```{r setup, include = FALSE}
options(htmltools.dir.version = FALSE, servr.interval = 0.5, width = 115, digits = 2)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE,
  comment = "#", strip.white = TRUE)

library(webexercises)

num_fitb <- function(x, digits = 2, width = 6) {
  a <- format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits)
  fitb(unique(c(a, sub(".", ",", a, fixed = TRUE))), width = width)
}

pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse, wbstats, vdemdata, estimatr, modelsummary
)

# Same joined pipeline as Exercise 1 (see its "Stuck?" box if the API is down)
Dat_co2 <- wb_data(c(co2 = "EN.GHG.CO2.PC.CE.AR5",
                     gdp = "NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD"),
                   start_date = 2000, end_date = 2026) %>%
  rename(country_text_id = iso3c, year = date) %>%
  select(country_text_id, country, year, co2, gdp) %>%
  drop_na(co2, gdp) %>%
  group_by(country) %>% filter(year == max(year)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(gdp_k = gdp / 1000)

Dat_vdem <- vdem %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(country_text_id, year, state_own_raw = v2clstown) %>%
  mutate(state_ownership = -state_own_raw)

Dat_meta <- wb_countries() %>%
  select(country_text_id = iso3c, region, income_level)

Dat <- Dat_co2 %>%
  inner_join(Dat_vdem, by = c("country_text_id", "year")) %>%
  inner_join(Dat_meta, by = "country_text_id") %>%
  mutate(income_level = fct_relevel(income_level, "Low income"))
```

*(Keep working in the R script from Exercise 1 — you already have `Dat` with `income_level`
releveled. If not, the starter code and the "Stuck?" box are in Exercise 1.)*

```{r fitmodels, include = FALSE}
ols_inc   <- lm_robust(co2 ~ income_level, data = Dat)
b_upper   <- coef(ols_inc)["income_levelUpper middle income"]
ols_state <- lm_robust(co2 ~ state_ownership, data = Dat)
pr <- predict(ols_state, newdata = tibble(state_ownership = c(-1, 1)),
              interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)$fit
p_market <- pr[1, "fit"]; p_state <- pr[2, "fit"]
```

1. **Write it yourself: a coefficient plot.** Fit `co2 ~ income_level`, `tidy()` it into a
   tibble, drop the intercept, and plot each coefficient with its 95% confidence interval
   (`geom_pointrange()` + `coord_flip()`).

`r hide("Hint")`
`tidy()` gives you `estimate`, `conf.low`, and `conf.high`. Filter out `"(Intercept)"`, then map `estimate` to `y`, the `term` to `x`, and add `geom_hline(yintercept = 0, ...)` as a reference line.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("R solution -> don't peek too early ;) !")`
```{r out.width='80%', fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6.5, results = FALSE}
plotdata <- lm_robust(co2 ~ income_level, data = Dat) %>%
  tidy() %>%
  mutate(term = str_remove(term, "income_level")) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)")

ggplot(data = plotdata,
       aes(y = estimate, x = reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "#901A1E", lty = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Income group",
       y = "Average difference in CO2 (t per person)\nvs. low-income countries") +
  theme_minimal()
```
`r unhide()`

2. Read your plot: compared with low-income countries, **upper-middle-income** countries emit
   about `r num_fitb(b_upper)` tonnes more CO₂ per person (two digits).

3. Which statement matches your coefficient plot?
`r mcq(c("All income groups overlap zero — none differs from low income", answer = "Every group emits more than low income, and the gap widens with income", "Only high-income countries differ from the reference"))`

4. **Write it yourself: a prediction plot.** Fit the **bivariate** model
   `co2 ~ state_ownership`, predict across a synthetic range of the socialism index, and plot
   the fitted line with its confidence ribbon. Mark two benchmarks with dashed red lines: a
   market-based economy (`-1`) and a state-run one (`+1`).

`r hide("Hint")`
The index runs from about −3 to +2, so build `fict_dat <- tibble(state_ownership = seq(-3, 2, by = 0.1))`, then `predict(ols_state, newdata = fict_dat, interval = "confidence")$fit`, turn it into a tibble and `bind_cols()` it back. Plot with `geom_ribbon()` + `geom_line()`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("R solution -> don't peek too early ;) !")`
```{r out.width='80%', fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6.5, results = FALSE}
ols_state <- lm_robust(co2 ~ state_ownership, data = Dat)

# Fictional countries spanning the observed range of the index
fict_dat <- tibble(state_ownership = seq(-3, 2, by = 0.1)) #<<
fict_dat <- predict(ols_state, newdata = fict_dat,
                    interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)$fit %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  bind_cols(fict_dat, .)

ggplot(data = fict_dat, aes(y = fit, x = state_ownership)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), color = "#901A1E", lty = "dashed") + #<<
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "State ownership of the economy (V-Dem, higher = more)",
       y = "Predicted tonnes of CO2 per person") +
  theme_minimal()
```
`r unhide()`

5. **A prediction does not have to be a plot.** You can also ask the model for a *single
   number*. Using the **bivariate** model `co2 ~ state_ownership` from Exercise 1, predict CO₂
   for a strongly market-based economy (`state_ownership = -1`, about where Denmark and
   Finland sit) and for a strongly state-run one (`state_ownership = +1`, about Russia and
   Angola). Build a `tibble()` with those two values and hand it to `predict()`.

`r hide("Hint")`
Same three steps as the plot, just with two rows instead of 120:
`tibble(state_ownership = c(-1, 1))`, then `predict(ols_state, newdata = ..., interval = "confidence")$fit`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("R solution -> don't peek too early ;) !")`
```{r}
ols_state <- lm_robust(co2 ~ state_ownership, data = Dat)

fict_two <- tibble(state_ownership = c(-1, 1)) # market-based vs state-run #<<

predict(ols_state, newdata = fict_two,
        interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)$fit %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  bind_cols(fict_two, .)
```
`r unhide()`

   The market-based country is predicted at `r num_fitb(p_market)` tonnes per person, the
   state-run one at `r num_fitb(p_state)` (two digits each).

6. Look at the two **confidence intervals** you just produced. Which is wider, and why?
`r mcq(c("They are the same width - the model is equally sure everywhere", answer = "The state-run one, because far fewer countries sit at that end of the scale", "The market-based one, because rich countries vary more"))`

`r hide("Why this matters")`
A prediction is only as good as the data behind it. Most countries in `Dat` sit on the
market-based side, so the model has seen plenty of them and its interval there is narrow.
Very few countries score high on state ownership, so out there the same model is guessing
from a handful of cases — and says so, honestly, with a much wider interval. This is exactly
the widening ribbon you drew in the prediction plot, read as numbers instead.
`r unhide()`

7. **Write one sentence** (as a `# comment`) that a reader of your term paper could follow,
   describing what the prediction plot shows. Then compare:

`r hide("Model answer")`
*Predicted CO₂ emissions rise with state ownership of the economy: a strongly market-based
country is predicted to emit about `r round(p_market, 1)` tonnes per person, a strongly
state-run one about `r round(p_state, 1)` — but the confidence ribbon fans out sharply on the
right, where very few countries actually sit, so the model is far less sure about that end.*
`r unhide()`

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

8. **Discuss with your neighbour** — three steps toward the *carbon divide*:

   a. Your two figures tell the same story two ways. Which is clearer for a reader who has
      *never seen a regression table* — the coefficient plot or the prediction plot?
   b. The prediction plot looks clean and confident. But in Exercise 1 that same slope
      **reversed** once the petro economies were dropped. Could you honestly publish this
      figure on its own?
   c. The countries emitting the **least** are often the most exposed to climate damage. What
      does that mean for reading a "positive slope" as *good* or *bad* news?

`r hide("Talking points")`
**(a)** The prediction plot needs no statistics vocabulary — it reads like a line on a graph;
the coefficient plot is compact but assumes the reader knows what a reference category is.
**(b)** No. The figure is perfectly *correct* and still misleading on its own: it is drawn from
a slope Exercise 1 showed is not robust, because the high-state-ownership end is populated by
petro economies. A plot cannot show you what it excluded — which is why the robustness check
belongs in the paper, not just in your script. **(c)** A
positive slope is neither good nor bad by itself — it is the *injustice* that the low emitters
bear the highest costs that turns the description into a research (and policy) agenda.
`r unhide()`

**Bonus (for the fast):** swap the coefficient plot's predictor from `income_level` to
`region`. Which reference category does R pick, and how would you change it to
`"Sub-Saharan Africa"`?

`r hide("R solution")`
```{r out.width='70%', fig.height = 4, fig.width = 6.5, results = FALSE}
# R uses the first factor level (alphabetical for a character vector) as the
# reference — so set it explicitly with fct_relevel(), as we did for income.
Dat <- Dat %>% mutate(region = fct_relevel(region, "Sub-Saharan Africa"))

lm_robust(co2 ~ region, data = Dat) %>%
  tidy() %>%
  mutate(term = str_remove(term, "region")) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = estimate, x = reorder(term, estimate))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "#901A1E", lty = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Difference in CO2 vs. Sub-Saharan Africa") +
  theme_minimal()
```
`r unhide()`
